rationale: This review synthesizes visual hallucination studies involving cholinergic dysfunction, Lewy pathology, visual attention and distributed brain circuits. It describes reports in medication-naive patients and an earlier levodopa challenge with no elicited episodes. The underlying observations are medication and mechanism leads, with no dried fig comparison.

Autopsy groups with Alzheimer disease, dementia with Lewy bodies, mixed disease, Parkinson disease dementia and controls were compared on regional tau, amyloid and synuclein burden. The design measures neuropathology by diagnostic group; dietary fig consumption and episode timing are absent.

This review considers glucose dysregulation, insulin resistance and proposed metabolic therapies in Parkinson disease. It cites separate brain glucose imaging comparisons in people with and without hallucinations. The group imaging results supply no dietary fig exposure or food-timed visual episode count.

The baseline polysomnography-confirmed isolated REM sleep behavior disorder cohort used cognitive assessments to identify mild cognitive impairment and describe clinical features. Its prodromal sleep and cognition comparisons do not measure dried fig consumption or response in Parkinson visual hallucination frequency.

The genetic-instrument analysis tested resting-state functional network traits against diagnostic risks in neurodegenerative disease. The main inverse-variance-weighted analyses reported no significant associations for the tested exposures. The instruments model brain network traits, with no culinary exposure or episode outcome.

The authors review central cholinergic contributions to Parkinson motor and nonmotor symptoms, including clinical hallucination data from cited studies. The article itself contains no meal intervention or independently measured dried fig and visual episode outcome.

The bibliometric analysis ranks 100 highly cited original papers on Lewy body dementia and summarizes publication and citation patterns. A ranked reference list yields no new individual exposure or symptom-frequency data.

Eleven participants with dementia with Lewy bodies, 12 with Parkinson disease and 11 age-matched controls completed clinical and rest-activity measurements. The study compares motor activity and circadian patterns across clinical groups. Core symptom information is clinical context and was not tied to dried fig or meal timing.

CoPPIs identifies protein interaction modules with differing co-expression across transcriptomic groups. The analytic outcome is differential correlation and pathway representation, with no dried fig exposure or clinical visual event counts.

This narrative review follows levodopa pharmacology, motor benefit and complications across disease stages. Any oral drug absorption discussion concerns medication and diet broadly, without a dried fig intervention and visual hallucination frequency endpoint.

The PADUA-CESNE clinical series included 35 participants, 23 with Parkinson disease, and used ocular imaging alongside clinical characterization. Its measured endpoint is retinal layer structure, distinct from spontaneous visual episode frequency.

An observational Parkinson biomarker study compares color-discrimination performance and optical coherence tomography measurements of outer retinal structure. Visual discrimination and retinal anatomy are separate from spontaneous formed visual phenomena. Individual culinary intake is absent.

This review evaluates research models for Lewy body dementia and discusses which disease features they reproduce. The model comparisons do not test consumption of dried figs or measure clinical episode frequency.

This secondary appraisal surveys plant-origin Parkinson interventions and summarizes outcomes from cited models and trials involving other botanicals. The complete original contains no common fig or dried fig treatment with reported Parkinson visual episode frequency.

PPMI classified 25 Parkinson participants with a broad hallucination or psychosis item and compared them with 56 Parkinson participants without symptoms and 24 controls. The separate ICICLE-PD sample used a dedicated visual interview and a severity score combining frequency, duration and type. Resting connectivity and subsequent clinical measures were compared without dried fig or other food-timed episode counts.

Two institutional cases and 17 patients from 13 papers document visual phenomena in a neurosurgical Charles Bonnet context. Some episodes were restricted to visual field loss. These are different underlying conditions and there is no oral food comparison.

The authors review noncoding variants implicated by genome-wide and rare-variant studies in dementia, with strategies for prioritizing candidate variants. The reviewed exposure is genetic variation, with no dried fig or Parkinson visual episode-frequency comparison.

Education is used as a proxy for cognitive reserve in Parkinson dementia and comparison participants, and the analysis compares resting EEG alpha markers. Educational attainment and electrophysiology supply neither food exposure nor visual episode frequency.

This report presents a multidisciplinary German Parkinson care approach. Nutrition support is a service component alongside other care, without item-level dried fig intake, an ingredient contrast or counted visual events.

The comparison concerns performance of assays for detecting abnormal alpha-synuclein in clinical material. Assay behavior or disease classification does not supply a culinary exposure or within-person episode outcome.

The comparison uses MRI in 32 Parkinson participants with visual hallucinations and 33 without them. The regression explicitly uses presence versus absence. The anatomic findings address group status without an ingredient exposure or a counted change in frequency.

The isolated REM sleep behavior disorder cohort compares basal forebrain imaging with controls and tracks later clinical diagnoses. Diagnosis progression and structural imaging provide no dried fig or meal-timed visual event comparison.

The systematic review includes people without dementia at enrollment and studies subsequent diagnoses of dementia with Lewy bodies, Parkinson disease dementia or broader Lewy body dementia. It evaluates prior visual symptoms as possible predictors, without a dried fig comparison or post-meal episode outcome.

Groups of people with Parkinson disease with and without hallucinations were compared on imaging measures of networks involving the amygdala and nucleus basalis of Meynert. The association is based on clinical group status. The food exposure, temporal attribution and episode frequency required for the frozen claim were absent.

The study included 372 people with Parkinson disease. It recorded 114 with one or more minor phenomena and 55 with visual hallucinations, with overlap. These counts describe people and clinical phenotypes, rather than the number of episodes after food consumption.

Two imaging analyses of isolated REM sleep behavior disorder track clinical progression and phenoconversion. The hallucination and psychosis scale appears as a clinical characteristic. No dated dried fig consumption or ingredient-specific visual episode comparison is reported.

The review describes diagnostic MRI and FDG-PET patterns across neurodegenerative diseases. Imaging distributions and differential diagnosis are its evidence scope. It collects no new dietary exposure or symptom episode comparison.

The clinical database identified 38 people diagnosed with dementia with Lewy bodies among 5,518 patients and summarized presenting characteristics. Diagnostic prevalence and symptom presence in that case series give no dried fig or visual event frequency comparison.

The 103-person Parkinson cohort uses sarcopenia screening and follows falls. Its nutritional and functional context is useful for understanding the cohort; the prospective outcomes are falls and recurrent falls, not dried fig or hallucination frequency.

The retrospective study extracts Capgras misidentification and other clinical features from Lewy body disease records, with matched imaging subsets. Co-reported visual hallucinations and the delusional misidentification phenotype are distinct observations. There is no fruit exposure or post-intake episode rate.

The main structural connectivity cohort compares 62 Lewy body spectrum participants, 46 people with Parkinson disease and stable cognition, and 23 healthy controls. MRI connectivity gradients characterize diagnostic groups without individual dried fig exposure or a visual episode-frequency endpoint.

A postmortem study of 371 Lewy body disease cases measures regional mitophagy markers and neuropathological burden, including analyses by genotype. It measures tissue and pathology rather than an ingested ingredient and clinical episodes.

The Find-DLB clinical referral cohort enrolled 144 eligible participants, with one excluded before diagnosis. Diagnostic classification and core features are documented at the specialist evaluation. The report supplies no measured fig intake or exposure-linked event rate.

This review compares fluid biomarkers and related diagnostic strategies in neurodegenerative disorders. Assay interpretation and differential diagnosis do not estimate clinical symptoms after a culinary exposure.

The clinical sample has 93 Parkinson outpatients, 55 without hallucinations and 38 with minor phenomena. The group comparison uses visual-to-semantic assessments. Those task measures and a history of minor phenomena do not provide repeated visual event counts after a meal.

A patient report and literature review describe parkinsonism associated with variants of VPS13C. Clinical and genetic observations refer to an individual disorder course. Dried fig intake and a timed visual outcome were not assessed.

The GBA1 literature review brings together genomic, transcriptional, protein and lipid findings in Parkinson disease. The synthesis addresses genotype and molecular pathways, without a culinary ingredient intervention or visual frequency result.

The meta-analysis evaluates noninvasive brain stimulation and measured cognitive and neuropsychiatric outcomes in Parkinson and atypical parkinsonian disorders. The tested interventions are stimulation modalities. The pooled cognitive and symptom-scale comparisons contain no dried fig exposure contrast.

Diffusion imaging compares a perivascular clearance proxy among Lewy body dementia, Parkinson cognitive groups and healthy controls. The biomarker analysis distinguishes diagnostic samples and image metrics from exposure-timed visual episodes.

Six population-based incidence cohorts contribute 883 participants to pooled Parkinson prognosis estimates. Endpoints include mortality, dependence and dementia. The cohorts' pooled outcomes provide no isolated dried fig exposure or visual episode-frequency measurement.

The experiments distinguish locomotion, staring, eye-tracking and responses in a pharmacological mouse model. Observable behaviors are proxies for an inferred state and carry no patient account of spontaneous visual episodes. The original does not administer dried fig.

This perspective compares clinicopathological and mechanistic patterns in LRRK2- and GBA1-associated Parkinson disease across the Lewy body spectrum. Genotype and pathology are the subject, with no fig ingestion or visual event count.

The preclinical study follows animal behavioral and retinal or pathway changes over time. Motor and depressive-like behavior have their own assays, with no human episode reports or dried fig exposure.

Resting high-density EEG compares 33 early dementia with Lewy bodies participants with 21 controls. Visual hallucination and REM sleep behavior status are examined separately in relation to alpha-band connectivity. There is no monitored fig exposure or change in the number of visual episodes.

The clinical sample from NCT03661125 comprised 18 people with Parkinson disease without hallucinations and 20 meeting Parkinson psychosis criteria. A dedicated interview characterizes visual phenomena. The experiment compares visual mismatch EEG and model-based connectivity, with no food intervention or food-timed clinical episode rate.

Ten observational studies of continuous subcutaneous levodopa strategies contributed to the review. Motor effects and reported neuropsychiatric adverse events concern medication exposure and heterogeneous follow-up, without a dietary ingredient comparison.

This review describes genetic susceptibility and variants across Lewy body dementia. Cited phenotype associations provide no independent culinary exposure measurement or count of visual episodes after food.

The tissue series maps amygdala pathology in 48 donors: six incidental Lewy body disease, 18 Parkinson disease, nine dementia with Lewy bodies and 15 Alzheimer disease with Lewy bodies. Regional protein accumulation provides no exposure-timed clinical event measurement.

The MEG analysis relates resting brain activity and cognitive fluctuations across Lewy body and Parkinson groups. The clinical visual descriptions do not identify a dated food exposure or compare visual episode rates.

The analysis uses the Allen Human Brain Atlas and regional gene-expression data to investigate brain patterns in Alzheimer and Parkinson disease. It contains no participant-level fig exposure or visual episode-frequency endpoint.

The computational botanical study uses Centella asiatica, a species distinct from Ficus carica, and models candidate target pathways. Database compounds and predictions provide no measured fruit exposure or patient visual episodes.

A case of PINK1-related Parkinson disease describes timed plasma drug measurements and neuropsychiatric observations while infusion, oral levodopa and a COMT inhibitor were adjusted. Several medication changes preclude a single-exposure comparison. Dried fig was not an exposure.

The study compares self-reported cognitive complaints and clinical characteristics in 74 cognitively unimpaired people with Parkinson disease, 36 of whom reported complaints. Subjective cognition is distinct from visual episode frequency, and neither arm represents a fig exposure.

The 77-person advanced Parkinson chart review records seven new hallucination cases during subcutaneous levodopa prodrug infusion, usually distressing and at night. The table separately counts other psychiatric events and reports median time to first hallucination of 14 days. This is onset during a drug exposure with treatment adjustments, with no dried fig intake or counts of repeated episodes.

The umbrella review includes 16 systematic reviews of repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation for Parkinson symptom domains. The tested treatment and review outcomes provide no dated culinary exposure or clinical visual episode-frequency comparison.

The study uses PPMI structural scans and item 1.2 during screening or early follow-up as a proxy for hallucination-related status. The item does not separate all visual subtypes and modalities. MRI-derived volume and presence or absence of the broad proxy do not provide food-timed episode frequency.
